paper.title_en: Fluctuation modes in the initial state of heavy-ion collisions: from 2D to 3D hybrid simulations
paper.abstract_en: This dissertation investigates how the initial stages of relativistic heavy-ion collisions shape the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) and the observables measured experimentally. Particular attention is given to the initial state and pre-equilibrium dynamics, which constitute the main sources of uncertainty in hybrid simulations. The first part of the dissertation reviews the framework underlying state-of-the-art hybrid simulations and the numerical tools used in phenomenological analyses. The second part studies the matching between pre-equilibrium evolution and viscous hydrodynamics. Since commonly used conformal kinetic-theory descriptions are inconsistent with the non-conformal hydrodynamic equation of state, an entropy-density matching prescription is proposed. This prescription reduces the artificial bulk pressure generated at the switching time and improves the consistency of the hybrid framework. The third part develops a mode-by-mode decomposition of initial energy-density profiles to isolate fluctuation modes and quantify their contributions to final observables. Applied to Pb-Pb collisions across centrality classes and extended to a fully three-dimensional O-O collision system, the method shows that initial fluctuations survive hydrodynamic evolution and leave measurable imprints on final observables. In O-O collisions, fluctuations can dominate over geometric effects from the impact parameter, demonstrating that intermediate-sized systems are not simply scaled-down versions of large systems. Overall, these results provide tools for constraining the early stages of heavy-ion collisions and for understanding how fluctuations propagate through the QGP evolution.
